newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - Australia retail, BOPS, registrations.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Australia retail, BOPS, registrations.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Statistics released three sets of data on Friday -- first quarter balance of payments, April retail trade and motor vehicle registrations.
Retail trade fell 1.7 percent against an expected 0.5 percent rise and 0.3 percent fall in March.
April motor vehicle registrations fell 6.0 percent compared with a 1.3 percent rise in March and an expected flat outcome.
Balance of payments showed a A$4.587 billion deficit after the A$5.3 billion shortfall in the December quarter and compared with median forecasts for a A$4.8 billion deficit.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"These monthly numbers are notoriously volatile, but we did see retail sales level off late in the March quarter with a fall a month of March. So many were expecting that we might get a little bit of a rebound in the month of April, so a fall of this magnitude, approaching two percent, is quite a weak number. So it doesn't set consumer spending off to a strong start in the June quarter."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"Obviously the key ones were the retail sales figures. They were clearly much weaker than most people were expecting, and certainly suggest that the economy isn't racing away at a great pace yet. The net exports figures will probably see people revising up their GDP numbers a bit after the stocks figures yesterday and a one percent figure for GDP looks to be about the best guess at the moment."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"It certainly indicates weakness in the economy. It certainly throws open the prospect of further rate cuts. The economy is not going ahead in leaps and bounds. It's always pleasing to see the current account improve. But I don't think markets will react to that. The new car registrations will add to the bullish tone of the markets."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANK:

"I think they're pretty disappointing. I would have expected a better retail trade number than that. I would have also expected auto registrations to hold up a bit better. It's continuing a pretty patchy picture for the economy and very much justifies the decision by the Reserve Bank to move last week cutting rates. The signs we're seeing are that where we were seeing some improvement in the economy, it's not really following through, there's not substantial momentum building up there in response to rate cuts last year. It's a pretty patchy recovery and these numbers pretty much confirm that."
ANNETTE BEACHER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"(Back to back falls in retail trade) match the back to back falls we've seen in housing finance and building approvals. It certainly is a surprise. We can't blame seasonal factors, we can't blame anything. It just may be a case of that spurt that we saw at the beginning of the year has now paused. There is no doubt growth will resume with the rate cuts we have seen, it's just taking a while to filter through into the hard dollars. It will definitely add to speculation of another cut, because it's a case of if the consumer doesn't come in, employment will never kick in."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"The figures are a bit soft. The retail trade is the most important one, and it does indicate that consumer began Q2 in a very soft fashion. Yesterday, the stocks and sales data suggested that there weren't any signs of strength in the economy in Q1. This suggests there aren't any signs in Q2 so far. There are no signs of a dramatic pick up in Q2 either. The long-awaited pick up in growth is proving more elusive than we thought."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"It (the retail sales figures) confirms that the March data was weak for an Easter sales period and underlying retail spending is not as strong as some people had thought after the Christmas slump. I mean we have basically seen it alternating between periods of slump, recovery, and softening again and my guess is that May will be the first clean reading we will get since November. It will certainly make the RBA feel more comfortable and relaxed about the easing they have already had."
